2027-03-01.title: Fourth Monday of the Great Fast
2027-03-01.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: The healing at the pool of Beth-zatha
2027-03-01.alt: Season of the Great Fast (Sauma Ramba).
2027-03-01.verse: When Jesus saw him lying there and knew that he had been there a long time, he said to him, “Do you want to be made well?”
theo: The fourth week of the Great Fast opens with a journey. God speaks to a man of seventy-five who has every reason to stay where he is: “Go from your country and your kindred and your father's house to the land that I will show you.” The promise is enormous, “I will make of you a great nation, and I will bless you, and make your name great, so that you will be a blessing”, but the map is blank. And the most important sentence in the reading is the shortest: “So Abram went, as the LORD had told him.” Notice what Abram does at every stop. At Shechem “he built there an altar to the LORD”, and near Bethel he pitched his tent “and there he built an altar to the LORD and invoked the name of the LORD.” Wherever his tent goes, an altar goes with it. The Syro-Malabar families who left Travancore in the last century to clear the forests of Malabar and the high ranges did the same: before the houses had proper roofs there was a small chapel, and the Holy Qurbana was offered among the stumps and the new rubber. The Great Fast asks each of us where God is asking us to go, and whether our tent still has an altar beside it.

Last Sunday we heard that one man had hidden plunder in his tent and that all Israel was weakened by it. Today the hidden thing comes out. Tribe by tribe, clan by clan, household by household, the lot narrows until Achan stands alone. Joshua's words to him are surprisingly gentle: “My son, give glory to the LORD God of Israel and make confession to him. Tell me now what you have done; do not hide it from me.” Achan answers: “It is true; I am the one who sinned against the LORD God of Israel.” The ending of this ancient story is grim, and the place is named the Valley of Achor, the valley of trouble. But the prophets did not leave it there. Through Hosea God promised to “make the Valley of Achor a door of hope” (Hosea 2:15). In the Church of Christ that promise is kept every time a sinner kneels in confession: the valley of trouble becomes a door of hope, and the one who says “I am the one who sinned” goes home forgiven.

Paul begins the great chapters of Romans on Israel with tears: “I have great sorrow and unceasing anguish in my heart.” He loves his own people, and he lists their gifts with pride: “to them belong the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the giving of the law, the worship, and the promises; to them belong the patriarchs, and from them, according to the flesh, comes the Messiah.” The Church has learned from him to speak of the Jewish people with reverence, never with contempt. In the Gospel Jesus goes to a pool where the sick lay waiting for the water to be stirred. One man had been ill “for thirty-eight years.” Jesus asks him what sounds like a strange question: “Do you want to be made well?” The man does not say yes; he explains why it has never worked: “Sir, I have no one to put me into the pool when the water is stirred up.” Jesus does not need the pool. “Stand up, take your mat and walk.” Later he finds the man in the temple and adds: “See, you have been made well! Do not sin any more, so that nothing worse happens to you.” When John writes that “the Jews” began to persecute Jesus, he means certain religious authorities in Jerusalem, not the Jewish people as a whole, for Jesus, his mother and all his apostles were Jews (Catechism 597). Halfway through the fast, the same question is put to us: do you want to be made well, or only to explain why you are still lying by the pool?
outline: Ask: do I want to be made well, or do I prefer my explanations?
A journey with an altar at every stop.
Achan's valley of trouble and the door of hope.
Thirty-eight years by the pool, and one word from Jesus.
“Do you want to be made well?”
live: Name one sin or habit you have lived with for a long time, and bring it to confession before Palm Sunday.
Keep an altar beside the tent
Wherever you are this week, at home, in a hostel or abroad, set apart one corner and one fixed time for prayer.
2027-03-01.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you saw the man lying by the pool and knew how long he had waited. Look on us too, and ask us again whether we want to be made well. Give us the faith of Abram to go where you send us, the honesty of a sinner who confesses, and the courage to stand up and walk. Turn every valley of trouble in our lives into a door of hope. Amen.
altar: The Holy Qurbana is the altar Abram carried in hope: wherever the Church pitches her tent, the Son offers himself to the Father, and the sick are told once more, “Stand up, take your mat and walk.”

quick: Abram went as the Lord told him, and built an altar wherever he camped.
Achan confessed; Hosea promises that the valley of trouble will become a door of hope.
Jesus asks a man ill for thirty-eight years: do you want to be made well?
2027-03-01.action: Name one long-standing sin or habit and take it to confession before Palm Sunday.
2027-03-01.question: Do I really want to be made well, or have I grown used to lying by the pool?

family.explain: There was a pool in Jerusalem where sick people waited for the water to move. One man had been ill for thirty-eight years, longer than most of our parents have been alive! Jesus asked him: do you want to be well? Then Jesus said: stand up, pick up your mat and walk. And he did! Jesus can heal what has been sick in us for a long time.
family.intention: We pray for those who have been ill for many years, and for those who look after them.
family.ask: Ask: “Is there something in our family that has needed healing for a long time? Let us ask Jesus about it tonight.”

illus: An old man in Thamarassery, who came to the Malabar hills as a boy in 1952, used to tell his grandchildren about the first year. The family had no house, only a shelter of bamboo and palm leaf. But his father and the neighbours spent their first Sundays building a small chapel of mud and thatch, and a priest walked up from the valley once a month to offer the Holy Qurbana there. “We had nothing,” the old man said, “but we had an altar. That is why we stayed, and that is why we are still Christians.”

pm.open: Lord Jesus, you ask us whether we want to be made well. Here we are; heal us. Amen.
share: Go from your country (Genesis 12:1). Where is God asking me to go, or to let go?
Make confession to him; do not hide it (Joshua 7:19). What have I hidden from God for too long?
Do you want to be made well? (John 5:6). What excuses do I give instead of saying yes?
pm.resp: Lord, stand us up and make us walk.
interc: For the Church, a pilgrim people that carries the altar wherever she goes.
For migrants and settlers, that they may keep their faith in new lands.
For the Jewish people, first to hear the word of God, that they may grow in faithfulness to his covenant.
For those who have been ill for many years, and for their carers.
For our group, that we may not hide our sins but bring them to the light.
pm.close: Father, you called Abram and he went; you healed the man by the pool with a word. Call us, heal us, and make us walk in your ways. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear friends, God says to Abram: go from your country and your kindred and your father's house to the land that I will show you (Genesis 12:1). Abram is seventy-five, the map is blank, and yet he goes. At every place he pitches his tent, he builds an altar. A Christian life is a journey with an altar at every stop.

Achan had hidden stolen things in his tent. When the truth comes out, Joshua says: my son, give glory to the Lord and make confession; do not hide it from me (Joshua 7:19). The place of his punishment was called the Valley of Achor, the valley of trouble. But God promised through Hosea to make the Valley of Achor a door of hope (Hosea 2:15). Confession is that door.

Paul speaks of his people Israel with great sorrow and great love, for to them belong the covenants, the worship and the promises, and from them comes the Messiah (Romans 9:4–5). We learn from him to honour the people of the first covenant.

By the pool lies a man who has been ill for thirty-eight years. Jesus asks him: do you want to be made well? (John 5:6). He answers with an excuse. Jesus answers with a command: stand up, take your mat and walk. Halfway through this fast, Jesus asks us the same question. Let us not answer with excuses. Amen.
kids: Children, a man had been sick for thirty-eight years, and Jesus asked him: do you want to be well? Then Jesus said: stand up and walk, and he did! Is there something you would like Jesus to make well in you? Tell him tonight.

intro: Theme: “Do you want to be made well?”
Abram's journey with an altar, Achan's confession, Paul's love for his people, and the man by the pool who was told to stand up and walk.

sub: A call with a blank map.
q: Now the LORD said to Abram, “Go from your country and your kindred and your father's house to the land that I will show you.
By faith Abraham obeyed when he was called to set out for a place that he was to receive as an inheritance; and he set out, not knowing where he was going.
points.apply: Set apart one place and one fixed time for prayer wherever you are this week.

sub: Do not hide it from me.
The valley of trouble becomes a door of hope.
q: Then Joshua said to Achan, “My son, give glory to the LORD God of Israel and make confession to him. Tell me now what you have done; do not hide it from me.”
Therefore confess your sins to one another, and pray for one another, so that you may be healed.
points.apply: Make a careful examination of conscience and go to confession before Palm Sunday.

points.h: Stand up, take your mat and walk
q: then the lame shall leap like a deer, and the tongue of the speechless sing for joy. For waters shall break forth in the wilderness, and streams in the desert;
Jesus said to him, “Stand up, take your mat and walk.”
points.apply: Name the excuse you give most often, and replace it this week with one act of obedience.

concl: God calls us to go, to confess, and to stand up.
Abram went, Achan confessed, the sick man walked: halfway through the fast, it is our turn.
2027-03-01.resolve: This week, answer Jesus' question with a confession and one concrete step.
